new_statements.rule_in_words: In the (polysynthetic) verb, primary stress falls on the first heavy syllable (long vowel or closed syllable, coda s counting) of the stem, i.e. the domain following the inflectional and instrumental prefixes, which are never stressed; by Talmy's account a stem with no heavy syllable would take final stress. Analysis rests on Talmy's 1972 verb data (speaker Selina LaMarr) and Talmy's unpublished phonological notes.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on alternating syllables on both sides of the primary-stressed syllable (attributed to Talmy's notes).
new_statements.exceptions: Instrumental prefixes never bear stress; coda s after a short vowel makes the syllable heavy for stress ([44]); the separate 'first-syllable heavy' restriction does not interact with stress ([53]). CONFLICTING EARLIER ANALYSIS: Olmsted 1958 (IJAL 24:219, sec. 4) treats stress as phonemic with three degrees (ordinary/strong/contrastive) and gives no positional rule; Olmsted 1961 (IJAL 27:91, sec. 2.2) says 'The one unpredictable aspect of the hortative is the place of stress', dividing verbs into endoaccentual (stress on the root) and exoaccentual (stress on final -ja:) classes, and (4.42) lists roots/affixes that 'always have the stress' -- i.e. lexical/morphological stress on Olmsted's Hat Creek data (speaker Ike Wilson).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the verb STEM (root + directional/derivational suffixes, excluding inflectional and instrumental prefixes) within the sentential verb word; all examples are inflected verb words from Talmy 1972 in broad-phonetic transcription. Nothing is said about nouns or citation forms of non-verbs. Source is a conference handout ('sketch'), explicitly preliminary and partly relaying Talmy p.c./notes.
new_statements.identity_note: Good 2004 analyses Talmy's 1965-70 data from Selina LaMarr (Atsugewi proper); Olmsted 1958/1961 describe the Hat Creek (Atsuge) dialect of Ike Wilson only and explicitly exclude the Apwaruge / Dixie Valley dialect. All refer to glottocode atsu1245 (no Glottolog dialect sub-codes used). Note the analytic conflict: Olmsted = phonemic/lexical stress (endo- vs exoaccentual verbs); Talmy/Good = predictable, weight-sensitive within the verb stem.

sources.note: Based on Talmy 1972 data and Talmy's unpublished phonology notes: instrumental prefixes never stressed; 'Stress is marked on the first heavy syllable of the stem'; coda s counts for weight; if a stem had no heavy syllable stress would be final (Talmy p.c.); secondary stress on alternating syllables on both sides of the main stress (Talmy notes); 'The stem is the domain of, among other things, stress'.

sources.citation: Olmsted, David L. 1961. Atsugewi Morphology I: Verb Inflection. International Journal of American Linguistics 27(2): 91-113. (sec. 2.2, 4.42)
sources.note: Sec. 2.2 (p. 91): 'The one unpredictable aspect of the hortative is the place of stress. Accordingly, verbs may be divided into two classes: endoaccentual (those which show the stress on some part of the root) and exoaccentual (those which show the stress on the final -ja:)'. Sec. 4.42: certain affixes/roots 'always have the stress', forms with more than one stress are 'not unusual'; stress 'only morphemically predictable'. I.e. lexical/morphological stress in Olmsted's analysis.

sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: online with a university library login (also: harvard online access (harvardkey); publisher (doi, likely paywalled))
sources.note: Sec. 4: 'Atsugewi has three phonemic degrees of stress: ordinary (...'unstressed' and left unmarked), strong stress /'/ and contrastive stress'; some utterances have only ordinary stress (t?spa: bark, namistaq cloud), some only strong (tata father); contrastive stress appears where strong stress usually is. Stress treated as phonemic; NO positional rule given. Hat Creek dialect, speaker Ike Wilson.
